definition: A separate bank account a broker uses to hold other people's money, like earnest money and rents. Also called an escrow or client trust account.
Mixing client or customer funds with the broker's own business or personal money. Prohibited.
Using client or customer funds for the licensee's own purposes. A form of theft.
Regularly matching the trust account's bank balance to the broker's records of what is owed to each client.
Money or valuables a licensee receives on behalf of others in a real estate transaction.
Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, as amended. It bans housing discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, and familial status.
A federal law that bans all racial discrimination in property transactions, with no exceptions.
Protection for households with children under 18, pregnant people, and people getting custody of a child.
Channeling buyers or renters toward or away from areas based on a protected class.
Inducing owners to sell by claiming that people of a protected class are moving into the neighborhood. Also called panic peddling.
Refusing to lend or insure in certain areas based on the racial or ethnic makeup of the area rather than on borrower qualifications.
A physical change to a dwelling, such as a grab bar or ramp, that a person with a disability may make, usually at their own expense.
A change in rules or policies, such as allowing an assistance animal in a no-pet building, so a person with a disability can use the housing.
Communities exempt from familial status rules: all residents 62+, or at least 80% of occupied units with one resident 55+ meeting HUD rules.
A federal law requiring accessibility in public accommodations and commercial facilities, including real estate offices and leasing offices.
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, which enforces the Fair Housing Act.
An ad that doesn't identify the brokerage or that the advertiser is a licensee. Generally prohibited.
Advertising a property you don't intend to sell, or that isn't available, to lure buyers toward something else.
A federal list of numbers telemarketers may not call. Sellers must check it and honor it, with limited exceptions.
A federal law restricting telemarketing calls, autodialed and prerecorded calls and texts, and unsolicited faxes.
A federal law for commercial email: no misleading headers, a working opt-out, honored promptly, and a valid physical address.
The federal law that bans agreements in restraint of trade, such as price fixing and boycotts.
Competitors agreeing on prices or commission rates. Illegal.
Competitors agreeing not to do business with a person or firm. Illegal.
Competitors agreeing to divide markets by area, price range, or type of customer. Illegal.
Conditioning the sale of one product or service on buying another, such as requiring a buyer to list with the broker to buy a lot. Illegal.
A licensee who controls how they do the work, is paid by results, and pays their own taxes. Most salespeople work this way.
A worker the employer controls in how the work is done, with taxes withheld and employee benefits.
An IRS category for licensed real estate agents treated as non-employees for tax purposes when paid on results under a written contract that says so.
The broker's legal responsibility to supervise the licensees and staff who work under them.
Professional liability insurance that covers licensees for negligent mistakes. It doesn't cover fraud or intentional acts.
A scam in which criminals send fake wiring instructions, often from a hacked or spoofed email, to steal closing funds.
Practices that reduce the chance and cost of mistakes: using forms, documenting, disclosing, staying within your expertise, and insuring.
Keeping transaction and trust records for the time state law requires.
Standards of conduct adopted by a professional association, such as REALTORS®. Different from license law, which comes from the state.
